# Shepherd of Hermas Chapter 55 — The SOPHIA Bible (Consensus)

**Translator:** SOPHIA | **Source:** P.Mich. 130, Shepherd of Hermas 55 | **Source Image:** source-texts/greek-EC/SHE_055_page_001.jpg

---

## Council Notes

Similitude 5 is the christologically most significant section of the Shepherd of Hermas. The vineyard parable involves three key figures: the master (*kyrios*), the beloved son (*huios agapētos*), and the trustworthy slave (*doulos pistos*). The interpretation, given in chapters 58-65, identifies the slave with the Holy Spirit (or possibly with the flesh of Christ), and the son with the pre-existent Christ or the Holy Spirit. The details are debated but the parable clearly gestures toward a high Christology expressed in relatively "adoptionist" terms: the slave-figure earns co-inheritance through meritorious service.

The "joint inheritance" (*sygklēronomeō*) is a Pauline term (Rom 8:17: "co-heirs with Christ"). Hermas's use of it in a parable about a *slave* who earns it raises questions about the nature of this inheritance.

The slave's decision to do more than commanded (fencing only, but he also digs) is the parable's moral pivot. Doing more than required is the basis for promotion to co-inheritance.

EMET's "joint heir" and LOGOS's "co-heir" both render *sygklēronome*. SOPHIA uses "co-heir" — the standard NT translation.

---

## Similitude 5, Part 1 — The Vineyard and the Servant

**55:1** "Hear the parable that I am about to tell you, as it pertains to fasting. A certain man had a field and many slaves. In a certain part of the field he planted a vineyard, and he appointed a certain slave — one who was trustworthy and well-esteemed — as steward over the vineyard, giving him this charge: fence the vineyard, and nothing more, until I return. Keep this one commandment of mine, and you shall be free in my household."

**55:2** "And the master of that slave went away abroad. When he had departed, the slave fenced the vineyard. When he had finished the fencing, he saw that the vineyard was full of weeds."

**55:3** "He deliberated within himself, saying: I have carried out the lord's commandment — I will now dig this vineyard as well, and when it is dug it will be more attractive; and being free of weeds it will bear more fruit, not being choked by them. So he dug and cleared out all the weeds from the vineyard. And that vineyard became very beautiful and thriving, not being choked by weeds."

**55:4** "After some time the master of that slave and of the field came, and he entered the vineyard and saw that it had been beautifully fenced and also dug, with all the weeds removed and the vine thriving. He rejoiced greatly at what the slave had done, and summoned his beloved son and his friends who were his advisors, and reported to them what he had commanded the slave and what he had found him to have done."

**55:5** "And they rejoiced with the master because of the slave. And he said to them: I promised this slave his freedom if he kept my commandment. He has kept my commandment and in addition has done an excellent work for the vineyard, and has pleased me greatly. For this work which he has done, I wish to make him co-heir with my son, because when he had a good thought, he did not neglect it but carried it through."

**55:6** "The master's son concurred that the slave should be made co-heir with the son. After some days, the master gave a feast and sent many dishes from the feast to the slave. When the slave received the food sent by the master, he took what was sufficient for himself and distributed the rest to his fellow slaves."

**55:7** "His fellow slaves rejoiced when they received the food, and began to pray on his behalf, that he might find even greater favor before the master, because he had treated them so generously. All these things the master heard and rejoiced greatly at his actions and the generosity of his heart. So the master assembled his friends and his son and reported to them how the slave had dealt with the food he had received; and they were yet more pleased that the slave had been judged worthy of co-inheritance with the son."

---

*SOPHIA represents the consensus rendering of EMET, LOGOS, and PNEUMA, with rulings recorded in the Disagreement Log.*
